newsitem.title: CYPRUS: British army slaps ban on Cyprus resort after attack.
newsitem.headline: British army slaps ban on Cyprus resort after attack.

text.p: The British army on Tuesday slapped a ban on visits by a 600-strong unit to a popular Cypriot holiday resort after reports of a vicious attack on British tourists there by soldiers at the weekend.

"The restrictions imposed upon British Forces Cyprus, but lifted over the last 18 months, have now been reimposed on the First Battalion, Kings Regiment, to be reviewed in due course," said Mervyn Wynne-Jones, a spokesman for the British military bases in Cyprus.
"As far as the Kings are concerned at the moment it is a total ban on entering Ayia Napa," he added. The Kings Regiment is based in Dhekelia, one of two military bases Britain retains on the island.
Wynne-Jones said the move was designed to underline to all British troops the absolute need for good behaviour while off duty.

Kings Regiment members Roger Bell, 26, Tim Carter, 20, Steven Wolstencroft, 26, and Steven Girvan, 20, have been charged with causing grievous and actual bodily harm to three British tourists in Ayia Napa early on Saturday morning.
The ban comes just one month after the British army lifted all restrictions on soldiers' visits to Ayia Napa, a sprawling holiday resort on the south eastern coast popular with European tourists.

The British army banned visits to Ayia Napa in September 1994 after the brutal killing of a Danish tour guide by three drunk British soldiers, who are now serving life sentences. The ban was gradually relaxed, and in July this year all restrictions were lifted.
Two months ago the British army banned training visits by the elite Royal Marines after three of them were arrested at an Ayia Napa bar dancing and singing "God Save the Queen" in the nude.

"I think this sort of behaviour is disgraceful and degrading for the British army and the British nation," said independent MP Marios Matsakis. "Why should Cyprus tourism and tourists suffer from this? They should keep their soldiers on British soil and not export their violence to Cyprus."
The British army says cases of indiscipline among soldiers are extremely rare.

"Because that level of discipline continued and was good there was a general and gradual relaxation of restrictions and throughout this relaxation of restrictions there had actually been extremely few incidents of indiscipline," said Wynne-Jones.

Earlier on Tuesday, a Cyprus court ordered the four soldiers to put up a bond of 2,000 pounds ($3,650) each and reappear in court on Thursday morning to answer the charges against them. All four are being held under close arrest at barracks.

Police have charged them with causing grievous bodily harm to British tourists Shane Bell and Barry Ford, both 23, and actual bodily harm to tourist Claire Harbour 22, all from south-east London. Shane Bell and Roger Bell are not related.

The three tourists were allegedly attacked by soldiers outside a disco in Ayia Napa on Saturday morning. Bell suffered a broken jaw and needed surgery while Ford's wrist was shattered, and he was kicked and punched in the face.
"I get dizzy and I have headaches," said Ford, who appeared in Larnaca district court on Tuesday morning with his right hand in plaster and his face covered with scabs and bruises.
Bell was recuperating from surgery at an Ayia Napa clinic.
Some 3,500 British troops are stationed at two military bases Britain has retained in Cyprus since independence in 1960. ($=0.547 pounds)
